prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

I consider the woman’s choice in liberating a red dress with pale-green sandals. My penury depresses me into a staring contest with a melting ice cube. A friend excited my husband with an invitation to pilot a boat with powerful thrusters. My gift of chocolate in pink cellophane failed to make the blonde smile. Consequently, I remind the party-goers that Trans World Airlines painted a new night with nebulae. I could be happy in Alphabet City, buildings crumbling around my notepad. I could be happy sipping iced tea while admiring the seamless face of a pool. I could be happy gurgling back at an infant dribbling green saliva down his chin. I could be happy downing Absolut gimlets (ice-cold, no ice) in a neighborhood bar with pool players providing the music, or a hotel whose walls are laminated with mahogany and where tuxedos prevail. I could be happy with your hand on my waist as you try to identify the scent hollowing my throat. An entire landscape in Antarctica disappears, evaporates until salt becomes the only debris. There are keys to everything, even handcuffs. You could have been happy, too.

I reflect on the woman’s decision to free a red dress, paired with light-green sandals. My poverty sinks me into silently watching an ice cube dissolve. One of our friends thrilled my husband by asking him to steer a boat equipped with forceful thrusters. The chocolate I offered, wrapped in pink cellophane, did not bring a smile to the blonde woman’s face. So I tell the people at the party again that Trans World Airlines had colored a fresh night sky with nebulae.

I might find happiness in Alphabet City, with decaying buildings surrounding my notebook. I might be content drinking iced tea as I look at the perfectly smooth surface of a swimming pool. I might feel joy making bubbling noises back to a baby while green drool runs down his chin. I might be happy drinking very cold Absolut gimlets—served without ice—in a local bar where people playing pool supply the soundtrack, or in a hotel lined with mahogany laminate, where tuxedos are the norm. I might be happy with your hand resting at my waist while you try to name the fragrance opening a hollow in my throat.

outputs.L3:
The speaker reflects on a series of moments marked by desire, poverty, social encounters, and unsuccessful attempts to create or sustain joy. These memories and imagined scenes move through different emotional landscapes, suggesting a life spent searching for happiness in people, places, and experiences. Yet each attempt seems incomplete, as though pleasure is always shadowed by disappointment or distance.

Happiness is imagined in many settings. It might be found in the rough vitality of Alphabet City, in the ease of poolside leisure, in the dim energy of bars, or in the temporary comfort of hotels. It might appear through travel, luxury, nightlife, or intimate companionship. The speaker seems to believe that happiness can emerge almost anywhere, whether in moments of glamour or in ordinary encounters, as long as the right feeling or connection is present.

At the same time, the images of movement, pleasure, and abundance contrast sharply with an underlying sense of dissatisfaction. Travel and luxury do not guarantee fulfillment; nightlife and social encounters do not necessarily lead to closeness. Even scenes that should suggest freedom or indulgence carry a feeling of emotional distance. The speaker appears to be surrounded by possibilities for pleasure while remaining unable to fully inhabit them.

The text therefore presents happiness as something real but unstable. It is possible, but it depends on fragile circumstances: where one is, whom one is with, and whether a moment of connection can be sustained. Happiness appears briefly, often as an image or a possibility, but it can vanish just as quickly. It is shaped not only by wealth, pleasure, or escape, but by human closeness and the ability to feel present within an experience.

By the end, the tone becomes more elegiac. The closing lines evoke loss, escape, and regret, as if the speaker is looking back on someone who has gone elsewhere or slipped out of reach. There is a sense that happiness might have been possible not only for the speaker, but for another person as well. This final suggestion deepens the sadness of the text: joy was imaginable, perhaps even attainable, but it remained uncertain, fleeting, and possibly missed.
outputs.L4:
The text presents a fragmented and dreamlike meditation on longing, poverty, social alienation, and the fragile idea of happiness. Rather than moving through a clear, linear narrative, it unfolds in surreal vignettes that feel like memories, fantasies, and observations breaking into one another. These fragments create a world where ordinary details become strange and emotionally charged. Images of hunger, cold, distance, and material lack stand beside moments of beauty, tenderness, or imagined escape, producing vivid sensory contrasts. Through this contrast, the text suggests that poverty is not only a physical condition but also an emotional and social one: it separates people from comfort, from belonging, and often from one another.

At the same time, the text does not entirely deny the possibility of happiness. Happiness appears in glimpses—through imagination, desire, brief encounters, or the hope that life might still become different. Yet these moments never feel secure. They are unstable, temporary, and easily lost. The characters or voices in the text seem to reach toward connection and fulfillment, but what they find is often absence, misunderstanding, or disappearance. This makes happiness feel less like a permanent state than a passing illumination, something briefly seen and then withdrawn.

By the end, the text’s sense of missed connection becomes especially powerful. The closing mood suggests that what has been lost is not only a person, an opportunity, or a specific moment, but also a larger possibility of being understood and saved from loneliness. The disappearance at the end therefore feels both personal and existential. It speaks to an individual experience of abandonment or failure, while also pointing toward a broader human condition: the fear that our desires may remain unanswered, that our lives may pass unseen, and that happiness, though imaginable, may always remain just out of reach.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem in the first person about jealousy, money troubles, parties, travel, and imagined happiness, using vivid details like a red dress, pale-green sandals, melting ice, chocolate in pink cellophane, TWA, Alphabet City, Antarctica, and handcuffs.
counterfactuals.output:
I wore the red dress because I wanted to look like a wound that had learned to dance.

At the party, the rooms were full of melting ice and people laughing through their teeth. Someone had arranged chocolate in pink cellophane on a silver tray, little parcels of sweetness shining like bribes. I took three and hid them in my purse beside a notice from the bank, folded and refolded until the numbers looked like insects.

You arrived with her.

She had pale-green sandals and the kind of hair that made weather seem obedient. I watched your hand find the small of her back, and jealousy rose in me like a city seen from an airplane window—lit, impossible, expensive. I imagined my heart in handcuffs, rattling against its own ribs.

All night I pretended to be elsewhere.

I was on TWA, crossing a blue-black ocean with a gin and tonic sweating in my hand. I was in Alphabet City, stepping over roses growing from cracked pavement, paying rent with counterfeit moons. I was in Antarctica, where desire wore a white coat and said nothing, where every kiss froze before it could betray me.

But really I was by the punch bowl, watching the ice surrender.

Money had been leaving me for months: through envelopes, through meters, through the little mouths of taxis, through the bright windows of stores where mannequins looked happier than saints. I wanted to buy a life with clean sheets and no unpaid bills, a kitchen full of oranges, a lover who would turn toward me as if I were the only country not at war.

Instead, I smiled.

I laughed when someone told a story about Paris. I nodded when someone said happiness is a choice, as if it were a hat in a shop, as if I had not tried on every color and found them all too small. In the mirror over the mantel, I saw myself duplicated among bottles and candles: red dress, tired eyes, mouth painted into obedience.

Outside, the streetlights trembled. Somewhere, planes were crossing oceans. Somewhere, people with money were sleeping beneath heavy blankets, dreaming in well-heated rooms. Somewhere, in Antarctica, a blue iceberg calved into the sea with the sound of a drawer full of silverware being dropped.

You kissed her shoulder.

I unwrapped another chocolate and let the pink cellophane cling to my fingers like a torn flag. The sweetness collapsed on my tongue. For one second, I imagined happiness clearly: not as you, not as money, not as applause at a party, but as a door opening inside me onto a warm room where no one was counting, no one was chosen, no one was left standing with melting ice in her glass.

Then the vision closed.

I went on smiling, because that is what the doomed do when they are well dressed.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a lyrical, fragmented monologue in the style of a late-20th-century New York literary narrator, beginning with observations at a party and moving into repeated “I could be happy…” fantasies before ending with a melancholy address to “you.”
counterfactuals.output:
At the party the women stand in little constellations, all wrist bone and cigarette ember, laughing at something that has already vanished. Men lean in doorways with their drinks held low, as if the ice might overhear them. Someone has put Miles Davis on and then forgotten him. The trumpet keeps walking through the rooms alone.

There are orchids in a vase on the mantel, expensive and faintly obscene. There is a bowl of limes no one will cut. A girl with silver eyelids is telling a story about Berlin, or betrayal, or a restaurant where the chef refused to serve her after midnight. The story changes each time I pass her. The city is pressed against the windows, black and glittering, all appetite.

I am holding a glass of something pale. I am not drinking it. I am listening to names drop and break on the parquet floor.

Outside, taxis go by like small decisions.

I could be happy in a room above a bakery, waking at five to the smell of bread and sugar burning at the edges. I could own two blue bowls, one cracked, and a plant that forgives me. I could stand barefoot by the window and not think of anyone’s mouth.

I could be happy in a town with one movie theater, where the marquee is always missing a letter, where rain makes the sidewalks shine like old patent leather. I could know the pharmacist by name. I could buy peaches in a paper bag and eat them over the sink, juice running down my wrist, no one watching.

I could be happy with a man who does not ask me what I mean when I say I’m tired. A man who fixes lamps. A man who sleeps heavily and without dreams. We would have a dog named after a saint. We would misplace our ambitions under the bed and sweep around them.

I could be happy alone, entirely alone, in a white apartment with no history. A mattress on the floor. One spoon. One towel. A table facing the wall. I would write letters and never mail them. I would learn the names of ships. I would let the phone ring until it became weather.

I could be happy as someone else, perhaps. Someone with a clean laugh. Someone who does not turn every kindness over in her hand looking for the blade. Someone who can leave a party before midnight and not feel the whole city closing behind her like a fist.

At the party, a man kisses another man’s wife beside the bookshelves, and everyone pretends to be studying the spines. The hostess has lost an earring. The ice is gone. The trumpet stops and begins again, wounded, gorgeous, bored.

And you—  
you are not here, which is the only way you know how to be everywhere.

You are in the hallway mirror when I pass it. You are in the pause before laughter. You are in the ash at the bottom of someone else’s glass. I carry you carefully, absurdly, like a match through wind.

If I leave now, the elevator will smell of perfume and rain. The doorman will nod as if I am expected somewhere. I will step into the street and the city will open its wet black mouth.

And I will go home, you know.  
Not to you.  
Never quite to you.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an experimental paragraph that feels like a collage of overheard sentences, luxury-brand details, emotional alienation, and apocalyptic imagery; include Absolut gimlets, mahogany hotel walls, pool players, a baby with green saliva, and the line “You could have been happy, too.”
counterfactuals.output: The Absolut gimlets arrived sweating on a lacquered tray while somebody behind me said the markets would open like a wound, and the mahogany hotel walls shone with the false depth of old money, with brass sconces, with the smell of citrus peel and rain-dark wool. “Don’t look at me like that,” a woman whispered into her phone, her Chanel chain slipping from one shoulder, while across the bar the pool players bent over green felt as if divining the end of the world from numbered planets. A baby in a white pram coughed up green saliva and everyone pretended it was pesto, or envy, or some new organic supplement from Zurich. Outside, ash drifted down over the valet stand; inside, the ice kept ticking in our glasses. Your hand was near mine but not touching it, Cartier watch face blank as a moon, and the news on mute showed towers of smoke, horses loose on a freeway, a minister crying under studio lights. “You could have been happy, too.” Someone laughed then, too loudly, and the cue ball cracked against the eight, and for one second every beautiful thing in the room looked borrowed, flammable, already gone.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dense poetic prose piece about a woman reflecting on missed happiness and social discomfort, with recurring images of ice, alcohol, clothing, airports/airlines, urban decay, Antarctica, keys, and handcuffs.
counterfactuals.output:
She kept thinking happiness had come dressed incorrectly, in the wrong coat, with a hem damp from street slush and a loose button clicking like a tooth. It had stood beside her at parties, smelling faintly of gin and airport carpet, while she mistook it for another obligation: another hand to shake, another glass to hold, another joke to understand too late. By the time she turned toward it, the room had shifted, the music had gone thin, the ice in her drink had collapsed with a small glacial sound, and everyone else seemed fluent in a language made of laughter and teeth.

She had always been awkward among people, as if born wearing invisible handcuffs: wrists polite, gestures shortened, affections detained. Dresses made her feel fraudulent; trousers made her feel armored; every blouse became evidence. In mirrors she saw not a woman but a traveler delayed indefinitely, tags on her luggage, face lit by the merciless blue of departure screens. Airlines had promised movement, elevation, escape, yet every airport was the same sealed winter: bars open at dawn, children crying in terminals, men asleep beneath advertisements for tropical beaches, women repainting their mouths in reflective windows while jets lifted like silver verdicts beyond the glass.

She remembered the cities she had lived in as a sequence of damaged locks. Apartment doors swelling in the rain. Mailboxes pried open. Subway gates coughing sparks. Keys lost in coat linings, dropped through grates, left on bedside tables in rooms she would never enter again. Outside, whole neighborhoods molted into rust and plywood; laundromats glowed all night like aquariums of exhausted clothing; liquor stores flashed their red signs over cracked pavement; pigeons picked at bread in the dirty snow. She had walked through it all with a paper cup of something burning in her hand, feeling the alcohol descend like a small elevator through her body, stopping at each floor of grief.

There had been chances, she supposed. A man laughing gently as he shook ice into two glasses. A friend who touched her sleeve and asked her to stay. A winter morning when the city looked almost forgiven, all its broken cars and blackened stoops softened under snow, and she could have believed in beginning. But she had turned away, as she always did, toward some imagined Antarctica of the self: immaculate, uninhabitable, white beyond weather, a continent where no one asked the wrong questions because no one came close enough to speak. She had made a virtue of coldness and called it clarity. She had made exile look tailored.

Now she understood that loneliness was not a locked room but a ring of keys she carried without trying any door. Happiness had not been grand; it had been domestic and badly lit, sitting with its shoes off, thawing at the edge of the bed. It had been the second drink refused, the coat accepted, the invitation survived. It had been the body unfastening itself from fear, the wrists slipped free of their shining cuffs, the plain shirt warm from another body, the boarding pass torn up before the gate was called. It had been possible, perhaps, in the ruined city, under the cheap ceiling, beside the melting ice.

And still she stood there, older now, holding a glass she did not want, listening to cubes strike one another like little polar catastrophes. Outside, planes crossed the night invisibly, carrying strangers over oceans and weather. Somewhere Antarctica kept its blue crevasses open like mouths that never spoke. Somewhere a lost key glittered in a gutter, furred with frost. She adjusted her collar, smiled at someone approaching, and felt again the old panic buttoned neatly beneath her clothes—then, beneath that, fainter but still alive, the warmth of all she had missed, burning patiently as alcohol, as shame, as a lamp left on in a city no one had yet abandoned.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a strange, elegant piece of flash fiction narrated by someone at a party, combining mundane social details with dreamlike associations, and use the repeated phrase “I could be happy” several times near the middle.
counterfactuals.output:
At the party, everyone wore shoes that seemed chosen by committee: brown loafers, silver heels, boots with polite buckles, sneakers that had been forgiven for something. I stood by the table of cut vegetables and listened to a man explain mortgage rates to a woman whose earrings were tiny golden ladders.

The apartment belonged to Lena, or to Lena’s husband, or to some mutual calendar where we all appeared briefly before being erased. There was art on the walls, large and pale, like weather seen from under anesthesia. Someone had brought a dog, though no one admitted it. Now and then a small warm flank brushed against my calf, and when I looked down there was nothing but the rug, full of red vines and blue animals.

In the kitchen, a bowl of ice sweated into its own reflection. A girl in a green dress asked if I was still “doing the archival thing,” and I said yes, though I had never done an archival thing in my life unless memory counted, unless counting counted. She nodded as if I had described a country she’d once fled.

The music was quiet but determined. It moved behind the conversations like a servant carrying knives.

I could be happy, I thought, watching a lemon slice sink in my glass.

I could be happy, if happiness were only this: standing upright, being asked whether I wanted more wine, recognizing faces just late enough to seem mysterious.

I could be happy, I could be happy, I could be happy, said the refrigerator, said the ice, said the invisible dog nosing through the coats on the bed.

Near the middle of the evening, everyone gathered on the balcony to see the moon, which had risen enormous and low over the neighboring roofs. It looked less like a moon than like a plate someone had eaten from very carefully. A man named Paul said, “That’s atmospheric distortion,” and his wife touched his sleeve with the tenderness reserved for facts that have become ill.

Below us, traffic slid along the avenue. Each car carried a person toward something ordinary—milk, medicine, an argument, a blue-lit room. I imagined lifting the roof from every building and finding the same party repeated forever: olives in bowls, women laughing too brightly, men checking their phones in the hall, a child asleep under a mountain of coats, dreaming that the coats were bears and that the bears were his ancestors.

Lena passed me a napkin printed with cranes. “You’re very quiet,” she said.

“I’m listening,” I told her.

“To what?”

I almost said: to the chandelier breathing. To the cheese softening into prophecy. To the dead making room for us at the edges of mirrors. Instead I said, “The music.”

She smiled, relieved to be among the living, and went to answer the door.

Later, someone spilled red wine on the pale carpet. A circle formed. Advice descended. Salt was summoned, club soda, towels, expertise. We all knelt around the stain as if it were a small country newly discovered and already in trouble. For a moment our heads bowed together, and I felt an elegant sorrow pass through us—not personal, not yet historical, simply the sorrow of matter changing shape.

When I left, the hallway was empty. From behind Lena’s door came laughter, then the sound of a glass breaking, then applause. In the elevator mirror my face looked borrowed, expensive, due back by morning.

Outside, the moon had climbed higher and become ordinary. My phone had no messages. A taxi passed, yellow and lit from within, like a thought refusing to stop.

I walked home carrying the party in me: the ladders, the lemons, the vanished dog, the stain blooming darkly under all that salt.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
